summary: Follow-up to the June 29th incident where Aegis experienced degraded latency and token errors during a traffic spike. We walked through the postmortem findings, clarified mitigations implemented, and agreed on next steps: run controlled benchmarks on Dedicated, update customer runbooks, and test failover/canary flows. Aegis wants quantifiable latency/cost tradeoffs and a validated rollback path before resuming production traffic ramp.
topics: Root cause (KV cache eviction + autoscale boundary)
Mitigations applied (patch, autoscaling tweaks, cache sizing)
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jamal (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood CSM); Ethan, Leah, Sanjay (Aegis)

Summary (auto-generated): Postmortem follow-up after June 29 incident. Focus on mitigations, test plan, and runbook updates.

[00:00] Maya: All right hi everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off, is this still a good 15 to 45 minute window?
[00:06] Ethan: Yeah good here, thanks Maya.
[00:08] Jamal: Hey team. Quick agenda 

[00:15] Leah: That sounds good. We mostly want to make sure the runbook reflects the real rollback steps and that the canary won't hit the same edge case.

[02:05] Jamal: Quick recap: On June 29 we saw a 3x traffic spike around 17:22 UTC, sequence lengths averaged 1.8k tokens because of a batch of long reports. Two things converged - the KV cache for a hot prefix got effectively thrashed, and autoscale boundary hit hard so additional replicas didn't come up fast enough. The combination increased tail latency and some token-generation errors surfaced.
[02:38] Ethan: When you say KV cache thrash, do you mean eviction caused cache misses which caused regen of large key values?
[02:45] Jamal: Yeah basically. Our runtime keeps a KV cache per model shard, and with heavy long-sequence traffic we had more unique prefixes and the cache sizing was too small for the working set. That produced a lot of cold starts for the decoder and increased compute per request. Couple that with short autoscale cooldowns and we got a capacity gap.

[04:12] Leah: Just to call out, we saw 504s at the LB at 17:29, approx 7 minutes after spike start. That matches what your telemetry shows?
[04:20] Jamal: Correct, our traces show increased queuing and then a few requests timed out at the service edge. Some spans had misattributed service names in the trace, apologies for that - the trace mapper had a naming bug so it looked like Speaker 1 in some of the traces.

[06:00] Maya: Okay thanks. What mitigations did Redwood push in the immediate window?
[06:08] Jamal: We pushed two short-term mitigations same day: raised KV cache target size for the model group and temporarily tightened request rate limits per route to prevent thundering-herd from a single client. We also increased the autoscale headroom (lowered target CPU to trigger scale earlier) and deployed a minor fix to the runtime to avoid a pathological degen path when cache misses coincide with long sequences - that was a code path that amplified latency.
[06:40] Ethan: Did any of those require redeploy or restart that could cause disruption?
[06:44] Jamal: The cache sizing change is dynamic and applied without restart. Autoscale headroom was a config change, rolled out via config push - we did a rolling config reload, no full cluster restart. The runtime patch required a rolling deploy of the serving version - small pods replaced over ~18 minutes. We tried to minimize disruption.

[08:30] Sanjay: On the runtime patch, is that now in the mainline? Will it be part of the pinned model version we have on Dedicated?
[08:36] Jamal: Yes it's in the release branch and we've cut a stable build. We'll publish the exact build hash and ensure your Dedicated pool can pin to that version. There might be a mismatch name in your console showing Redwood Dedi 2.1 instead of Redwood Dedicated - sorry transcription-ish or UI glitch.

[10:20] Leah: For the canary and rollback plan, we need explicit playbook steps - how do we detect and what exact signals cause rollback, plus an automated rollback if the canary fails.
[10:32] Priya: We're aligning on that - our proposed thresholds are 95th percentile latency > 500ms or error rate > 0.5% sustained for 3 minutes during canary. If triggered, automatic fallback to the previous model variant + scale-up of older variant is the plan.
[10:50] Ethan: Can we get those thresholds back in writing? Also cost tradeoffs if we force more headroom.

[12:00] Jamal: We'll send the thresholds and also a small cost delta estimate for different headroom settings - higher headroom increases reserved GPU hours, we can show token cost per hour vs. latency improvement.

[13:10] Sanjay: Question on security - you mentioned some telemetry traces had obfuscated names and the audit logs didn't show the config push details clearly; we need full audit for when config changes happened and by whom, for compliance.
[13:25] Maya: Understood. We'll share the audit log extract and full timeline. For private KMS usage we can also arrange a test to show KMS rotations, key access logs.

[15:05] Leah: On data residency - we had a concern about fallback region. If we failover to a different region, that could violate policy. Are failovers region-aware?
[15:14] Jamal: Yes, failover policies are region-aware. For your account we set policy to avoid cross-region fallback except as a last resort. We can add a hard guard so the failover only uses approved regions.

[16:40] Ethan: What's the plan for Dedicated vs Hosted? We were testing Dedicated to avoid noisy neighbors, but the incident still happened. Is there an architecture change needed?
[16:50] Jamal: Two notes - Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor risk but autoscale configs and cache sizing still matter. For Dedicated we recommend explicit pre-warming for peak windows (manual scale-up) and an increased cache allocation per shard. We're proposing a small footprint change: increase cache mem by ~30% and pre-warm capacity 10 minutes before known peak. That will reduce tail latency.

[18:20] Leah: Pre-warm is doable. We need a simple API call or console action to trigger pre-warm.
[18:26] Jamal: We have an API that can set min-replicas and prefetch the KV cache for a set of prefixes - we'll provide a short script that your SREs can run as a cron or integrate into deploy pipeline.

[20:00] Maya: Ok, about the controlled benchmark - we propose Redwood stand up a dedicated pool in our account (or a mirrored environment) and run the same traffic profile that caused the incident plus a few worst-case variations. We'll capture latency, tail, and cost.
[20:12] Ethan: We prefer the benchmark in our VPC copy for compliance reasons. Can Redwood run the benchmark inside our private deployment?
[20:20] Jamal: Yes, we can run it in your Private deployment, we just need KMS access for logs and a short infra window. There may be additional approvals for us to access your VPC - we'll coordinate with your infra team.

[22:10] Sanjay: A few nitty gritty items: 1) I want a timeline with exact config changes and timestamps, 2) confirm the patch release hash and the images used in the deploy, 3) show the trace that links 504s to queue depth.
[22:25] Maya: We'll send a timeline artifact and attach the trace links. Note traces may have occasional mislabels, we'll annotate them.

[24:40] Leah: Runbook language - we also need role-based steps, e.g., who calls PagerDuty, who runs the cache resize script, and who approves the rollback.
[24:50] Priya: We'll update runbook with owners and add a one-click rollback snippet that your infra can require sign-off for. We'll also add an emergency auto-fallback toggle if you want fully automated response.

[27:00] Ethan: One more question - does the runtime have any guard that rejects extremely long sequence requests to protect the system? We saw some clients send sequences >4k tokens.
[27:10] Jamal: We have optional sequence-length caps per route. We didn't have it enforced on the route that tripped. For canary we recommend enabling a soft cap with a warning threshold at 3k and hard cap at 6k to prevent runaway cost.

[29:30] Leah: Regarding audits - can you provide SOC2 evidence for change control around config pushes and deploys?
[29:40] Maya: Yes, we'll attach relevant SOC2 artifacts and change-control summaries. For any additional compliance proof we'll coordinate with your security team.

[31:15] Sanjay: About cost - what's the expected per-hour cost increase if we keep higher headroom in Dedicated?
[31:22] Jamal: Rough estimate: a 20% increase in baseline reserved GPUs yields roughly a 18-22% increase in hourly spend but cuts 95th percentile latency by roughly 30-40% for these workloads. We'll produce a short cost table.

[33:00] Maya: OK moving to next steps recap. We'll produce: mitigations doc and annotated timeline, the build hash and deploy image list, a runbook with owners and rollback steps, and schedule the benchmark in your VPC.
[33:12] Ethan: Good. When can we expect the mitigations doc?
[33:16] Maya: We aim to send by Friday 2026-07-23.

[34:40] Priya: I'll coordinate the canary schedule and invite list - propose July 30-31 or the week of Aug 3.
[34:48] Leah: We prefer July 30 if possible.

[36:00] Jamal: For the benchmark we'll need sample traffic, sequence length distribution and client labels. Leah can send logs with peak windows.
[36:10] Leah: I'll export and send a sanitized log sample by tomorrow.

[37:30] Ethan: One last concern is roll-forward vs rollback - we prefer rollback for stability but we want the option to roll-forward if a safe path exists. Document both.
[37:42] Priya: Noted, both will be documented.

[39:00] Maya: Any blockers we haven't covered?
[39:06] Sanjay: Just legal signoff for Redwood engineers in our VPC for the benchmark, we'll start that with procurement.
[39:12] Maya: OK we'll await the green light.

[40:30] Ethan: Thanks everyone. Appreciate the clear steps.
[40:34] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with artifacts and schedule.
[40:38] Jamal: Bye.
